name: Tatar
variety: Literary Tatar, based on the Central (Kazan) dialect, Cyrillic script
sources: Poppe, Nicholas (1963). Tatar Manual. Indiana University.
Berta, Árpád (1998). Tatar and Bashkir. In Lars Johanson & Éva Á. Csató (eds.), The Turkic Languages. Routledge.
Comrie, Bernard (1997). Tatar (Volga Tatar, Kazan Tatar) phonology. In Alan S. Kaye (ed.), Phonologies of Asia and Africa. Eisenbrauns.
contrasts: full vowels /i y u æ ɑ/ versus reduced (short, lax, centralised) mid vowels /ĕ ø̆ ŏ ɤ̆/, spelt е/э, ө, о, ы; the Volga vowel shift raised the old mid vowels and reduced the old high vowels
front versus back and rounded versus unrounded vowels
velar /k ɡ/ versus uvular /q ʁ/, predictable from vowel backness in native words but contrastive in Arabic and Persian loans
alveolo-palatal fricatives /ɕ ʑ/ (spelt ч, җ) where most Turkic languages have affricates
allophony: /ɑ/ is rounded [ɒ] in the first syllable and after [ɒ], with the rounding fading towards the end of the word
in native words к and г are uvular [q] and [ʁ] next to back vowels, velar stops [k] and [ɡ] next to front vowels
rounding harmony of the reduced vowels is not written: ы and е after о and ө of the first syllable are pronounced rounded (борын [bŏrŏn], төлке [tø̆lkø̆]), weakening further from the first syllable
reduced vowels are very short and may be devoiced or dropped between voiceless consonants and next to sonorants (кеше)
/l/ is velarised next to back vowels
в is [w] in native and Arabic words, [v] in Russian loans; /w/ is written у or ү after a vowel
/h ʔ/ occur in Arabic and Persian loans, /v ts tɕ/ and full /e o ɨ/ in Russian loans
ч and җ are affricates [tɕ dʑ] in western (Mishar) speech
phonotactics: no onset clusters in native words; Russian loans keep theirs
coda clusters are sonorant + obstruent (дүрт, кырк)
backness harmony in native words and suffixes; rounded vowels of non-initial syllables occur only through the unwritten rounding harmony
the letters ь and ъ do not stand for sounds of their own: they mark a front or back reading of neighbouring letters, a syllable break, or belong to Russian spelling

stress.type: fixed final by default, with morphological and lexical exceptions
stress.rule: Stress falls on the last syllable; unstressable suffixes and particles (negative -ма/-мә, question -мы/-ме, predicative personal endings) leave it on the syllable before them, second person imperatives and question words are stressed on the first syllable, and Russian loans keep their Russian stress.
stress.cues: not instrumentally studied in the sources used; the reduced vowels stay short even in the stressed final syllable

rhythm.vowel_reduction: lexical rather than stress-driven: the reduced vowels ĕ ø̆ ŏ ɤ̆ are short and centralised in every position and can be dropped in fast speech
rhythm.notes: The alternation of full and reduced vowels gives uneven syllable durations.

length.notes: No long versus short pairs of the same quality; the contrast is full versus reduced vowel. Sequences such as ий are pronounced long [iː]. Geminates occur in a few native words (илле 'fifty'), at morpheme boundaries and in loans. No published duration ratio is given here.

intonation.declarative: rise on the final stressed syllable of non-final phrases, fall at the end of the statement
intonation.yes_no_question: marked by the particle -мы/-ме; pitch is high on the syllable before the particle
intonation.wh_question: prominence on the question word, final fall
intonation.continuation: rise at the end of non-final phrases
intonation.accent_shape: rise to a high on the final stressed syllable
intonation.notes: Low confidence: no instrumental study of Tatar intonation was available to me; the entries follow the general pattern of the better described Turkic languages (Turkish, Kazakh).

problems: г next to front vowels becomes the velar fricative [ɣ] (the phoneme g is changed to Q), so гөл gives [ɣøl]; Tatar has the stop [ɡ] there and a fricative only in back-vowel words
ь and ъ are always read as a glottal stop (сәгать gives [sæʁɑtʔ]); in Tatar they are silent markers, and [ʔ] occurs only in a few Arabic loans
the unwritten rounding harmony of the reduced vowels is not applied (борын gives [borɯn])
stress is always final: unstressable suffixes, imperatives and question words are not handled (барма gives final stress)
Russian loanwords are read by the native rules: в is always [w], о and е are the reduced vowels, stress is final
t is the unaspirated base2 stop while p and k are the aspirated base1 stops
good: the reduced vowels е, ө, о, ы are shorter than the full vowels (length 110 against 180)
first-syllable rounding of а to [ɒ], carried on to the second syllable
к and л get uvular and velarised variants by vowel backness; ч and җ are [ɕ] and [ʑ]
я, ю, е choose front or back vowels by the harmony of the word; backness harmony otherwise follows from the spelling
the front vowels æ (ә), y (ү) and ø̆ (ө) are present

notes: The vowel list includes /e o ɨ/ and the consonant list /v ts tɕ h ʔ/, which occur only in loanwords. The degree of aspiration of the voiceless stops is not documented in the sources used.
